abstract:
This paper presents a computational model integrating transmural drug transport, smooth muscle cell contraction, nonlinear anisotropic material behavior, and residual stresses to investigate the effects of calcium channel blockers~(CCBs) on local stress distributions in atherosclerotic arteries.
  The balance of linear momentum is coupled with a three-dimensional reaction-diffusion equation for the drug transport.
  Smooth muscle contraction is modeled phenomenologically based on a chemo-mechanical model that incorporates the effects of stretch on intracellular calcium dynamics and calcium sensitization.
  A novel drug-tissue interaction model is proposed to capture the effects of CCBs on intracellular calcium and thus on smooth muscle contraction.
  Material parameters are identified by fitting to experimental data from the literature and finite element simulations are conducted on five exemplary atherosclerotic arterial geometries reconstructed from histological cross-sections.
  Simulation results show that although CCBs reduce the stresses in the media through reduced smooth muscle contraction, they shift load to the fibrous cap, whose stress increases in all five geometries (median of up to 28.9~kPa).
  This increase varies strongly between plaque morphologies and becomes smaller with lower smooth muscle tone before treatment, lower drug concentrations in the arterial wall and increasing axial pre-stretch.
  A blood pressure reduction of 10~mmHg already lowers it to a median of at most 3.8~kPa in four of the five geometries.
  Our findings suggest that CCBs may increase the rupture risk of vulnerable plaques with highly loaded fibrous caps under insufficient blood pressure reduction, which remains to be confirmed experimentally and clinically.
